title.en: Zeus Behind the Ram's Fleece: Why Amun Has a Ram's Face
title.zh: 拉姆皮毛後的宙斯：阿蒙何以有羊首

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (temple of the Theban Zeus, Amun)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（底比斯宙斯/阿蒙神廟）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.42 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 42

summary.en: Heracles begged to see Zeus, and Zeus did not desire to be seen: at last, flaying a ram, he held the head before his own and threw the fleece over himself, and so showed himself — hence the image of the Theban Zeus (Amun) wears a ram's face, and once a year the Thebans flay a single ram, drape its skin over the god's image, and beat themselves in lamentation over the beast.
summary.zh: 海拉克勒斯懇求一見宙斯，而宙斯不欲被見——終乃剝一公羊，執其首於己面之前，以羊毛皮覆身而現形——故底比斯宙斯（阿蒙）之像作羊面；底比斯人歲一剝羊，以其皮披於神像，眾皆擊胸哀悼此羊。

sensitivity.note: Ancient aition via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Now all who have a temple set up to the Theban Zeus or who are of the district of Thebes, these, I say, all sacrifice goats and abstain from sheep: for not all the Egyptians equally reverence the same gods, except only Isis and Osiris (who they say is Dionysos), these they all reverence alike... Now the men of Thebes and those who after their example abstain from sheep, say that this custom was established among them for the cause which follows: — Heracles (they say) had an earnest desire to see Zeus, and Zeus did not desire to be seen of him; and at last when Heracles was urgent in entreaty Zeus contrived this device, that is to say, he flayed a ram and held in front of him the head of the ram which he had cut off, and he put on over him the fleece and then showed himself to him.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.42.

passages.text: Hence the Egyptians make the image of Zeus into the face of a ram; and the Ammonians do so also after their example, being settlers both from the Egyptians and from the Ethiopians, and using a language which is a medley of both tongues: and in my opinion it is from this god that the Ammonians took the name which they have, for the Egyptians call Zeus Amun. The Thebans then do not sacrifice rams but hold them sacred for this reason; on one day however in the year, on the feast of Zeus, they cut up in the same manner and flay one single ram and cover with its skin the image of Zeus, and then they bring up to it another image of Heracles. This done, all who are in the temple beat themselves in lamentation for the ram, and then they bury it in a sacred tomb.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.42.

title.en: The Greek Lie of Busiris: Heracles Was Not Sacrificed in Egypt
title.zh: 布西里斯謊言辨：海拉克勒斯未嘗於埃及被祭

region.en: Egypt as imagined by Greek story (the sacrifice that never happened)
region.zh: 希臘故事想象中的埃及（未嘗發生之祭）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.45 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 45

summary.en: Against the Greek tale that the Egyptians crowned Heracles and led him out to sacrifice him to Zeus, Herodotus answers with law: the Egyptians, to whom it is not lawful to sacrifice even most beasts — swine, clean oxen and geese excepted — could never sacrifice human beings; 'Having said so much of these matters, we pray that we may have grace from both the gods and the heroes for our speech.'
summary.zh: 希臘人言埃及人曾加冠於海拉克勒斯、牽之就祭壇欲獻祭於宙斯——希羅多德以律法駁之：彼邦連多數畜類尚不可祭（豬與潔淨牛犢、鵝除外），豈能祭人？——『言及於此，惟願神與英雄宥我此言。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnographic polemic via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Moreover, besides many other stories which the Hellenes tell without due consideration, this tale is especially foolish which they tell about Heracles, namely that when he came to Egypt, the Egyptians put on him wreaths and led him forth in procession to sacrifice him to Zeus; and he for some time kept quiet, but when they were beginning the sacrifice of him at the altar, he betook himself to prowess and slew them all. I for my part am of opinion that the Hellenes when they tell this tale are altogether without knowledge of the nature and customs of the Egyptians.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.45.

passages.text: For how should they for whom it is not lawful to sacrifice even beasts, except swine and the males of oxen and calves (such of them as are clean) and geese, how should these sacrifice human beings? Besides this, how is it in nature possible that Heracles, being one person only and moreover a man (as they assert), should slay many myriads? Having said so much of these matters, we pray that we may have grace from both the gods and the heroes for our speech.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.45.

title.en: The Brick Pyramid Speaks: 'Despise Not Me in Comparison with Stone'
title.zh: 磚金字塔自銘：勿以我比石塔

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (the brick pyramid of Asychis by the lake)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（湖畔阿西基斯磚塔）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.136 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 136

summary.en: In the reign of Asychis money moved so slowly that a man might borrow against the mummified body of his father, losing his own burial and his family tomb if he defaulted; and the king, to surpass all before him, built a pyramid of bricks dug from the lake mud — with an inscription in stone on it: 'Despise not me in comparison with the pyramids of stone, seeing that I excel them as much as Zeus excels the other gods.'
summary.zh: 阿西基斯之世貨幣滯澀，乃立借貸之法：可以亡父之木乃伊作抵押；欠債者自身與族墓皆不得葬——王欲凌駕前王，乃以湖泥所取之磚築塔，塔上刻石銘曰：『勿以我比石塔而輕我：我之勝彼，如宙斯之勝諸神。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In this king's reign they told me that, as the circulation of money was very slow, a law was made for the Egyptians that a man might have that money lent to him which he needed, by offering as security the dead body of his father; and there was added moreover to this law another, namely that he who lent the money should have a claim also to the whole sepulchral chamber belonging to him who received it, and that the man who offered that security should be subject to this penalty, if he refused to pay back the debt, namely that neither the man himself should be allowed to have burial when he died, either in that family burial-place or in any other, nor should he be allowed to bury any one of his kinsmen whom he lost by death.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.136.

passages.text: This king desiring to surpass the kings of Egypt who had arisen before him left as a memorial of himself a pyramid which he made of bricks, and on it there is an inscription carved in stone and saying thus: 'Despise not me in comparison with the pyramids of stone, seeing that I excel them as much as Zeus excels the other gods; for with a pole they struck into the lake, and whatever of the mud attached itself to the pole, this they gathered up and made bricks, and in such manner they finished me.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.136.

title.en: The Twelve Kings and the Labyrinth: One Cup, One King
title.zh: 十二王與迷宮：一盃一王

region.en: Above the lake of Moiris, Middle Egypt (the labyrinth opposite the City of Crocodiles)
region.zh: 埃及中埃及莫伊里斯湖畔（鱷城對面之迷宮）

texts.period: Priests' account of the 12 kings (26th Dynasty prelude), recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.147-149 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 147-149

summary.en: Twelve kings divide Egypt and swear friendship on one oracle: he who pours a libation from a bronze cup in the temple of Hephaistos shall be king of all; they leave as a common memorial the labyrinth — twelve roofed courts, three thousand chambers, and under ground the sepulchres of the kings and of the sacred crocodiles, which Herodotus was not permitted to see; and it surpassed, he swears, all the works of the Greeks together, pyramids included.
summary.zh: 十二王分治埃及，共誓不相侵，蓋因一神諭：於赫菲斯托斯神廟以銅盂奠酒者必王全埃及；彼等共築迷宮以為紀念——十二座有頂庭院、三千間房室，地下則為諸王與聖鱷之墓，希羅多德不得入觀；彼自誓：此迷宮勝希臘一切建築之總和，金字塔亦不及。

sensitivity.note: Ancient foundation-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Being set free after the reign of the priest of Hephaistos, the Egyptians, since they could not live any time without a king, set up over them twelve kings, having divided all Egypt into twelve parts. These made intermarriages with one another and reigned, making agreement that they would not put down one another by force, nor seek to get an advantage over one another, but would live in perfect friendship: and the reason why they made these agreements... was this, namely that an oracle had been given to them at first when they began to exercise their rule, that he of them who should pour a libation from a bronze cup in the temple of Hephaistos should be king of all Egypt (for they used to assemble together in all the temples).
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.147.

passages.text: It has twelve courts covered in, with gates facing one another, six upon the North side and six upon the South, joining on one to another, and the same wall surrounds them all outside; and there are in it two kinds of chambers, the one kind below the ground and the other above upon these, three thousand in number, of each kind fifteen hundred... For the passages through the chambers, and the goings this way and that way through the courts, which are admirably adorned, afforded endless matter for marvel... Over the whole of these is a roof made of stone like the walls; and the walls are covered with figures carved upon them, each court being surrounded with pillars of white stone fitted together most perfectly.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.148.

passages.text: The upper set of chambers we ourselves saw, going through them, and we tell of them having looked upon them with our own eyes; but the chambers under ground we heard about only; for the Egyptians who had charge of them were not willing on any account to show them, saying that here were the sepulchres of the kings who had first built this labyrinth and of the sacred crocodiles. Accordingly we speak of the chambers below by what we received from hearsay, while those above we saw ourselves and found them to be works of more than human greatness. The pyramids also were greater than words can say... but the labyrinth surpasses even the pyramids.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.148.
